bio.en: Albert Cheng is one of the world's leading consumer growth leaders, having led growth and monetization at Duolingo, Grammarly, and Chess.com, where he applies an experiment-driven, user-value-focused approach to scaling beloved products.
bio.zh: Albert Cheng 是全球顶尖的消费增长领导者之一，曾在 Duolingo、Grammarly 和 Chess.com 主导增长与变现，用实验驱动、聚焦用户价值的方式规模化打造受人喜爱的产品。

summary.en: Albert defines growth as "connecting users to the value of your product" and uses an explore-and-exploit framework to balance finding the right mountain with climbing it well—surfacing a single insight across the product compounds wins, and while experiment win rates are often just 30–50%, breakthrough wins deserve a company-wide swarm. For freemium and consumer subscriptions, retention is gold: make the free product reflect the full value (Grammarly's sampled paid suggestions nearly doubled upgrades) and invest in resurrecting dormant users. AI accelerates growth work (text-to-SQL bots, AI prototyping), and chess.com pairs engines with LLMs for coaching; brand and mascots (Duo the owl) plus word-of-mouth virality (screenshot hotspots) combine powerfully with experimentation. Shifting a culture from zero to "1,000 experiments a year" relies on CEO buy-in, early wins, and a system (instrumentation, growth model) that matters more than the number itself.
summary.zh: Albert 把增长定义为「把用户连接到产品价值」，并用「探索与利用」框架平衡「找对要爬的山」与「有效爬那座山」——把单个洞察跨产品复利，胜率通常只有 30–50%，但突破性的赢要全公司 swarm。对 freemium/消费订阅，留存是金：让免费产品反映全部价值（Grammarly 抽样穿插付费建议让升级率近翻倍），并投资「复活」休眠用户。AI 加速增长工作（text-to-SQL 机器人、AI 原型），chess.com 用引擎+LLM 做教练；品牌与吉祥物（Duo 猫头鹰）和口碑病毒（截图热点）与实验结合是火箭燃料。把文化从零实验推向「一年一千实验」靠的是 CEO 支持、早期胜利，以及比数字本身更重要的系统（埋点、增长模型）。

(00:12:48): I can change the success rating, I could tweak some copy, change the color of some buttons, and so you now can take this experiment win and expand it out 10X across your organization and that's the kind of exploitation phase of it. So when done right, you can oscillate between the two until you saturate out of exploitation mode and then you encourage the teams to brainstorm and get more creative again.
turns.zh: 对，我最初是从我在 Grammarly 的工程搭档 Nermal 那听到「探索与利用」的，我想他其实上过一些 Reforge 的课。所以原始发明者可能是 Brian Balfour，我知道他上过你播客。但总之，它是个好概念。要点是：当你在探索模式，把它想成「找对要爬的山」；当你在利用模式，就像把资源聚焦在有效爬那座山上。对某些公司，我想给的警告是别在光谱一端花太多时间。如果你探索太多，团队会感觉有点太散弹，就试一百个不同的随机想法。贯穿线是什么？策略是什么？你怎么跨它们 pattern match 成功？如果你利用太多——那常是增长团队的 MO——它会导致饱和和停滞，你只是在局部最大化一个东西。即使这个探索与利用原则通常想成宏观的事，我更喜欢在「洞察」层面跟我团队工作。所以我给你个具体例子。我在 chess.com，我们的优先之一是鼓励棋手进步、学习和提高。我们有个 PM Dylan，他做所有学习功能。我们产品里最常用的学习功能叫「对局复盘」（game review）。你下一盘棋，结束后我们有个虚拟教练教你最糟的步、最好的步等等。他的工作是改善用户参与和留存。所以他在这探索阶段，想搞清楚怎么驱动更多那种活动？而他观察到的是，80% 复盘的人其实是在赢之后。而那对我们直觉很反……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, so there's a lot here to follow up on. One is the core piece of advice when you find something that works really well, find ways to build on that learning. One is here's an insight, it can apply to other parts of the product. "Hey teams, here's something we learned unexpected. Maybe this can help you. Also, just keep find more, run more experiments in the same zone." I imagine is a part of that.
turns.zh: 惊人。好，这有很多要跟进。一是核心建议：当你找到特别管用的东西，找方式建在那个学习上。一是这里有个洞察，能应用到产品其他部分。「嘿团队，这是我们意外学到的。也许这能帮你。还有，就继续找更多、在同区跑更多实验。」我猜那是其中一部分。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, exactly right. In my experience, the typical win rate, and I hate to use that term for experiments, is often something like 30 to 50%. Usually you're trying a bunch of things, a lot of hypotheses turn out not to be true, consumer products are very unpredictable like that, but when you do find a thing that breaks through the noise, and it could actually be a hugely losing experiment too, those are also super valuable. (00:13:58): Surfacing those across the company, the original PM running that experiment doesn't necessarily need to be the person that figures out what you should do for all the other parts of your product experience, but the onus is on them to clearly articulate what their hypothesis is, what they found such that then as a growth leader, I can encourage people to swarm around that and try a bunch of different ideas such that the success rate is up and the impact is up. So it's just oscillating back and forth between the two. That is the magic bullet.
turns.zh: 对，完全对。按我的经验，典型的胜率——我讨厌用那个词形容实验——常常在 30% 到 50%。通常你试一堆东西，很多假设结果不真，消费产品就是这么不可预测，但当你真找到一个突破噪声的东西，而且它也可能是一个巨大的失败实验，那些也超有价值。在公司里浮出那些洞察，跑那实验的原始 PM 不一定需要是搞清楚你该为产品体验其他部分做什么的人，但他们的责任是清楚阐明自己的假设是什么、发现了什么，这样作为增长领导，我就能鼓励人们 swarm 上去、试一堆不同想法，让成功率和影响都上去。所以就是在两者之间来回振荡。那才是 magic bullet。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think another takeaway here/something that I think about when I hear what you're saying is there's often a lot more wins in an area than people expect that you can continue to find wins and growth in something for a long time.
turns.zh: 我觉得另一个 takeaway、我听你说想到的，是一个领域里常比人们预期有更多胜利——你能在一个东西里持续找到胜利和增长很久。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Exactly right. Yes. At the end of the day, users, I think within a company sometimes you can have this siloed approach where you break apart the product experience in 50 different ways and distribute them across different teams, and you assume that users interact with each of the different features with a different mentality, but oftentimes that's actually not necessarily the case. And so sometimes, you can surface an insight that's more human psychology based that can resonate across the entire product experience. And so I think when you can find that, you can double down.
turns.zh: 完全对。对。到一天结束，用户——我觉得在公司里有时你会有这种筒仓方式，把产品体验拆成 50 种不同方式、分给不同团队，你假设用户用不同心态跟每个不同功能互动，但往往那其实不一定。所以有时你能浮出一个更基于人类心理的洞察，能跨整个产品体验共鸣。所以我觉得当你能找到那个，你就能加倍下注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People hearing this might feel like, "Okay, yes, find big wins and then find more." Is there something you find that helps you figure out when to explore versus when to exploit when you've exploited too far? Just like any heuristics or I don't know, ways of helping people guide them along this process of exploring and exploiting?
turns.zh: 听这个的人可能感觉「好，对，找大胜利然后找更多。」有没有什么能帮你判断什么时候该探索、什么时候该利用、当你利用太远了？就像任何启发式、或我不知道，帮人引导这个探索利用过程的方式？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: One thing that I try to focus on at a company of our scale of a chess.com, right? We're running roughly 250 experiments a year. So we're not the highest in the industry, but we run a decent volume. And so when that happens, I invest in these experiment explorer tools and we can talk about AI as well as another way to uncover and pick out these nuggets of wisdom, but basically, these explorer tools can allow me to look across the spectrum of experiments that are going on. (00:16:08): Try to figure out if there are patterns between the hypotheses and the learnings that are happening. And if I'm starting to see more and more experiments that are not statistically significant, that may be a signal to me to say, "Okay, we might've tried to exploit a little bit too far. There might not be as much juice to squeeze. Hey guys, let's get back to the table and brainstorm and be a little bit more divergent with our thinking."
turns.zh: 一件我尽量聚焦的，是在我们 chess.com 这种规模的公司，对吧？我们一年跑大概 250 个实验。所以我们不是行业最高，但量不错。所以当那发生时，我投在这些实验探索工具上——我们能聊 AI 作为另一种揭开和挑出这些智慧 nugget 的方式——但 basically，这些探索工具让我能看跨正在进行的实验光谱，试着搞清楚假设和正在发生的学习之间有没有模式。而如果我开始看到越来越多实验不统计显著，那可能是个信号对我说「好，我们可能利用得有点太远了。可能没那么多汁可挤。嘿哥们，回到桌前 brainstorm、让想法更发散点。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, let me follow this thread on AI and how you're using AI to help you figure this out. That is very cool. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 好，让我跟这个 AI 的线、以及你怎么用 AI 帮你想清这个。那超酷。讲讲。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: I think one of the latest things that we've been tinkering around with is this text to SQL capability. It's actually pretty powerful. We have this data request Slack channel where for the longest time, and this is still true today, people will toss in all sorts of just one-off questions. How many subscribers do we have in South Africa? Or how long did somebody play puzzles last month or something? (00:17:07): And these ad hoc questions, they often take a lot of human time to just go in and a data analyst needs to prioritize it and find time to go run the query. And yes, you can invest in self-serve tooling to improve at this, but also I found that AI is quite good at doing that first pass answer as well. And so we're working on training some of these Slack bots to essentially be the first party provider of a lot of these answers, which makes the company as a whole lot more data informed, I guess. (00:17:39): And I think what's also kind of interesting is that just human nature is that if you have a question that you feel like you might be a bit embarrassed to ask or you don't want to bother someone, you just don't ask the question. And so by the nature of having these tools, you get actually a pretty large explosion of questions being asked. And I think you see this in ChatGPT too, right? It's like just having a thing that you can converse with that you feel comfortable in makes a huge difference.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们最近在捣鼓的最新东西之一是这个 text-to-SQL 能力。它其实相当强。我们有个数据请求的 Slack 频道，最长一段时间、现在也还这样，人们会扔进各种一次性问题：「我们在南非有多少订阅者？」或者「某人上个月玩拼图玩了多久？」这些 ad hoc 问题常花很多人力去进、数据分析师得排优先级、找时间跑查询。而 yes，你能投在自助工具上改善这个，但我也发现 AI 做那第一遍答案也相当好。所以我们正在训练一些 Slack bot，基本作为很多这类答案的第一方提供者，这让公司整体更数据 informed，我想。而且我觉得也有点有趣的是人的本性：如果你有个问题觉得问了会有点尴尬、或者不想麻烦人，你就干脆不问。而通过这些工具的本质，你其实得到问题被问的相当大爆发。我觉得你在 ChatGPT 也看到这个，对吧？就是有个你能舒服对话的东西，差别巨大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, this is extremely cool. So is this something you build basically it's a Slack bot that gives you the SQL query or does it actually do the analysis for you?
turns.zh: 好，这超酷。所以这是你建的基本是个 Slack bot 给你 SQL 查询，还是它其实为你做分析？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: No, it does the analysis. Yeah.
turns.zh: 不，它做分析。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Whoa, so cool. Okay. Is this something you guys are going to release or is this just like somebody, you guys should just build this at every company?
turns.zh: 哇，太酷了。好。这是你们要发布的东西，还是就像——某人，你们该在每个公司都建这个？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: We should. It's a good idea.
turns.zh: 我们该。好主意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay. Well, there's an episode where everyone in the comments is like, "Open source this." So we'll see if that happens again. That is very cool. Are there other examples of that kind of stuff that you've done or seen?
turns.zh: 好。好。有期节目大家评论里都像「开源这个。」所以看那会不会再发生。那超酷。有别的你做或看到的那种例子吗？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: An adjacent example is a lot of the product managers, we're tinkering around with all sorts of different prototyping tools right now. It's just like go from an idea to a representative solution. Today, there's a lot of humans involved in taking an idea, writing up a spec, doing a review, doing design, et cetera. I'm sure you've interviewed plenty of people that have talked about this specific problem. (00:18:52): And so for us, we've invested a bit in at least carving out the main screens of our product experience, things like our onboarding flow, our home screen, our chessboard as an example, and building essentially AI prototypes of those using tools like a V0 or a Lovable. And when you have those foundational pieces, you can then share them with the rest of the company and they can use that as a starting point and then they can try to put their ideas on top of that and then they become a lot more discussable and hopefully testable relatively soon.
turns.zh: 一个相邻的例子是很多 PM，我们现在在捣鼓各种不同原型工具。就是从想法到一个代表性的解决方案。今天，把想法变方案有很多人参与——写 spec、做 review、做设计等等。我肯定你面试过很多人聊过这个具体问题。对我们，我们投了点，至少在切出我们产品体验的主屏幕，像引导流程、主屏、我们的棋盘为例，并用 V0 或 Lovable 这类工具基本建那些的 AI 原型。当你有那些基础块，你能跟公司其他人分享、他们能用那当起点、然后试着把想法放上面、然后它们变得更能讨论、希望相对快能测。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's in your AI stack along those lines?
turns.zh: 你那条线的 AI 栈里有什么？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: The PMs are mostly using V0. The designers love Figmas, they're using Figma Make. The engineers are using a combination of tools right now. So Cursor, Cloud Code, GitHub, Copilot. Marketing teams use all sorts of tools for translation, subtitles, content adaptations, et cetera. Customers support uses Intercom then. So there's quite a lot of tools that are used across the company. (00:19:50): I would say though that something that is annoying to me is that we haven't yet figured out the bridging from the tinkering to the workflow quite as seamlessly as I would like. And so each sub-function, even though the common I guess wisdom now is that AI is going to strip away these functional titles. It is true that based on your experience, you may gravitate to using a type of tool more. And if that tool isn't as interoperable with some of the other tools that you need to pass down the chain to actually ship it into production, at least at our scale. (00:20:24): I think for smaller startups, sure, PMs should just go ship it, but for us, we are still doing some handoffs between functions. I expect that to change over time and we are investing in some of design system components and MCPs and stuff to make it a little bit easier. But yeah, it's an investment and it takes time to smooth things out.
turns.zh: PM 主要用 V0。设计师爱 Figma，他们用 Figma Make。工程师现在用工具组合：Cursor、Claude Code、GitHub、Copilot。营销团队用各种工具做翻译、字幕、内容适配等等。客户支持用 Intercom 然后。所以公司里用的工具相当多。我会说 though 有件让我烦的是，我们还没搞出从捣鼓到工作流的桥接，像我想要那么顺。所以每个子职能，即使现在 common 智慧是 AI 会剥掉这些职能头衔，基于你的经验你确实可能倾向用某类工具更多，是真的。而如果那工具不能跟你往下传链真正要 ship 进生产需要的其他工具互操作——至少我们的规模。我觉得对小初创，当然，PM 该直接去 ship，但对我们，我们还在职能间做些 handoff。我预期那随时间变，我们在投一些设计系统组件和 MCP 之类让这事容易点。但对，它是投资、需要时间理顺。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to this topic of how things have changed and how you work as a product person, as a growth person across the companies you've been at. But first of all, I want to talk about another example of finding growth wins and monetization wins. Noam Levinsky, who is Chief Product Officer at Grammarly, you worked with him for a while while you were at Grammarly. He said that I need to ask you about the biggest monetization win that you found at Grammarly and how you discovered the opportunity.
turns.zh: 我想回到这个话题——事情怎么变、以及你作为产品人、增长人跨你待过的公司怎么工作。但首先，我想聊另一个找增长胜利和变现胜利的例子。Noam Levinsky，Grammarly 的 CPO，你在 Grammarly 时跟他共事一阵。他说我得问你关于你在 Grammarly 发现的最大变现胜利、以及你怎么发现那个机会。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: I had the pleasure of working with Noam and his product team at Grammarly. Some context first for those that don't use Grammarly. So Grammarly is an AI-powered writing assistant. And so typically, people will use it as a Chrome extension or a downloadable desktop client. And basically what it does is it overlays your writing with a bunch of different-
turns.zh: 我有幸跟 Noam 和他在 Grammarly 的产品团队工作。先给不用的朋友点上下文。Grammarly 是个 AI 驱动写作助手。通常人们把它当 Chrome 插件或可下载桌面客户端用。基本它做的是把你的写作叠上一堆不同的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I use it. I'm a big fan. I use it-
turns.zh: 我用。我是大粉。我用——

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Correction, so you're a big fan.
turns.zh: 更正，所以你是大粉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... And it saves my life.
turns.zh: ……而且它救我命。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Fantastic. Glad to hear that. Grammarly is a freemium business model, which means that over 90% of our users are on the free service and the rest of it pay for subscriptions essentially, right? And so one of the teams, they work on subscriber conversion, PM there is Kayla, that team is great and their job is to figure out the free to paid subscription path. (00:21:54): And so one of the realizations, one, is that we weren't actually tracking the events that well for the types of essentially suggestions that people were getting and how often were users seeing paywalls and stuff like that. That's kind of step number one. We have to put that instrumentation in. Step number two is that, "Hey, we noticed, actually first let me explain some of the logic." (00:22:18): So as a free user, you basically get these underlines across your writing and if you accept all of them, then you see the paywall and that encourages you to subscribe for more nuanced features. As a free user, the main things you get are spelling, grammar, they're basically correctness things. And as a paid user you get that, how do you improve your tone to be more empathetic? How do you improve your writing to be more clear? (00:22:40): How can you rewrite entire sentences, that type of thing. And so the observed behavior from all that tracking and data was that actually a very small percentage of our free users was deciding to accept all of their suggestions. They were more picking and choosing as they go, and I wonder if your experience is kind of similar too.
turns.zh: 太棒。高兴听到。Grammarly 是 freemium 商业模式，意思是超 90% 用户用免费服务、其余基本付订阅，对吧？所以其中一个团队做订阅转化，那的 PM 是 Kayla，那团队超棒、工作就是搞清楚免费到付费订阅的路径。一个 realization，一是我们实际上没很好追踪那些事件——人们得到的建议类型、用户多常看到付费墙之类。那是第一步，我们得把埋点放进去。第二步是「嘿，我们注意到——其实先让我解释些逻辑。」作为免费用户，你基本得到写作上的这些下划线，如果你接受所有，就看到付费墙、鼓励你订阅更细腻的功能。作为免费用户，你得到的主是拼写、语法，基本是正确性东西。作为付费用户你得到那个，加上怎么改善语气更共情、怎么改善写作更清晰、怎么重写整个句子那种。而从所有那些追踪和数据观察到的行为是，其实很小百分比的免费用户决定接受所有建议。他们更多边走边挑——我想你的体验也类似吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Definitely, yeah. I'm always like, "Wait, stop rewriting everything." Just like this part is wrong. I will fix it. Yeah, I'm very much a pick and choose.
turns.zh: 绝对，对。我总像「等等，停，别重写一切。」就这部分错了，我会修。对，我很挑。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Correction person.
turns.zh: 更正型的人。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: And then the second thing, which is I think equally if not more interesting is that I was at this company during this generative AI transformation, which is obviously still going on. And quite frankly, both the company brand as well as the lived product experience for most of the free users was that Grammarly was just a product to fix your spelling and grammar because those were the free suggestions we were showing people. (00:23:34): And so we decided to flip that on its head entirely and we said, "Okay, what if we actually sampled a number of different paid suggestions and interspersed them to free users across their writing?" Such that they were intermingled and we would provide a limited taste of what the paid offering had to provide. And on the surface, even though it's rational, the concern is that if we give too much of this away, then will people want to subscribe? (00:23:58): And we found completely that was not the case all of a sudden, people were seeing Grammarly as a much more powerful tool than they were before and our upgrade rates nearly doubled just through this change. And so I think this is interesting, just modernization learning that especially if you work on a freemium product, try to have your free product be a reflection of everything that your product can offer you. Obviously to an extent there's some costs involved with some of the paid features and things like that, but it generally will pay for itself if you're able to put your best foot forward and go do that. So that really worked well for us there.
turns.zh: 然后第二件，我觉得同样或更有趣的是，我在公司时正值生成式 AI 转型，显然还在进行。而且坦白说，公司品牌和大多数免费用户的真实产品体验是，Grammarly 只是个改拼写语法的产品，因为那些是我们给人看的免费建议。我们决定彻底翻转那个，我们说「好，如果我们其实抽样一些不同付费建议、把它们穿插给免费用户、铺在他们写作里？」这样它们交织，我们会提供付费产品能提供的有限尝鲜。表面看，即使理性，担心是如果我们给太多这个，人们还想订阅吗？我们发现完全不是那样——突然间人们把 Grammarly 看成比之前强得多的工具、我们的升级率几乎翻倍就靠这改变。所以我觉得这有趣，是现代化学习：尤其如果你做 freemium 产品，试着让你的免费产品反映你产品能提供的一切。显然在程度上有些付费功能有成本之类，但一般如果你能把最好的一面亮出来、去做了，它会 self-pay。所以那真的对我们很好用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this is what converted me to being a paid Grammarly subscriber. Wow, what a genius move. So essentially, it's here's a bunch of improvements, but you get three, I think max, and then it's like, "Okay, now you get upgrade."
turns.zh: 我觉得这就是把我转化成付费 Grammarly 订阅者的原因。哇，多天才的招。所以 basically，这是一堆改进，但你最多得三个，然后就「好，现在你升级」。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: It's basically a reverse free trial but in real time while you're writing as opposed to a time-based one. So we adopted some patterns that are in the industry, but molded it to Grammarly's specific use case.
turns.zh: 它基本是个反向免费试用，但是实时在你写作时、而不是基于时间的。所以我们采用了行业里一些模式，但 molded 成 Grammarly 的具体用例。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. I was going to ask, so it's not like a full trial, it's like a capped trial where you get a certain number of things and then you run out and then they get refreshed. I think once a day or something like that is what I found.
turns.zh: 对。我正要问，所以它不是完整试用，而是个有上限的试用——你得到一定数量的东西、然后用完、然后刷新。我想大概一天一次或类似频率，这是我发现的。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, you got it.
turns.zh: 对，你懂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Grammarly is the best/most devious at their upsells. I'm always just like, "God damn it, I'm so close to seeing an improvement, I just have to upgrade." And it's right there, it's right there where my mouse is.
turns.zh: 对。Grammarly 在 upsell 上是最厉害/最狡猾的。我总像「该死，我差点就看到个改进，我就得升级。」而且它就在那，就在我鼠标那。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, well, I'm not proud of being devious, but.
turns.zh: 对，嗯，我对狡猾不自豪，但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In really getting me to buy the thing. Good job. What was it? Kayla? Okay, nice job Kayla. It's very effective. I love that. Okay, so in terms of the free trial, I don't know, is there anything there of just, there's always this question of freemium, give things away and then there's pro account, there's like trial versus time. Some features are limited. I don't know, do you have for consumer subscription products like here's the way to go?
turns.zh: 在真的让我买这东西上。干得好。那是谁？Kayla？好，干得好 Kayla。非常有效。我爱。好，关于免费试用，我不知道，有没有什么就——一直有这个问题：freemium、把东西送出去然后有 pro 账户、有试用 vs 时间。有些功能受限。我不知道，对消费订阅产品你有「该这么走」的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, I think first of all, why do freemium subscription in the first place is a common question that I've joined all these companies that are freemium subscription. What do I like about it I guess? Well one, I think it ties really nicely to mission orientation of a lot of these companies. It's often like you want to spread the product as wide as possible because that's why the founders built the thing, right? (00:26:22): You're trying to improve education with Duolingo or Grammarly or Chess.com, these are meant to be widespread products with a really wide value proposition that fits globally. And so obviously, the lowest friction to that is going to be a free product. So that alone is part of it. Another part of it is that a lot of these products primarily grow through word of mouth and especially if you can build network effects in the product, like Duolingo has a bunch of social features or with Grammarly, they have a bit of a B2C2B play as well. (00:26:54): So you see Grammarly being used by teams and by companies and whatnot, and even if users are on the free plan, they still provide quite a lot of value in making sure that Grammarly can be purchased by a coworker or by a team member or whatever. So I think these things are usually why I lean toward make sure that the core value proposition that you're providing users is free and is permanently free and then you layer on a sampling or a taste of some of the premium features that are on top of it. That's usually the sweet spot that I've seen. (00:27:26): As to the trials, reverse trials type of thing, I think it largely depends. I think if you have especially a B2B feature where you may have some lock-in, reverse trials can be super powerful. You just want to get people in there. You don't need to ask for their credit card because they're using your CRM or they're investing quite a lot of time in building out material and content. And so by the time that window drops, you actually feel, "Oh man, I probably should keep this and start paying." I think for a lot of consumer products it's a little bit harder for that to work. And so I've typically seen more just normal free trials be the norm.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得首先，为什么先做 freemium 订阅，是我加入的这些公司都 freemium 订阅的常见问题。我喜欢它的什么？一是我觉得它跟很多这类公司的使命导向绑得很好。常常是你想把产品铺得越广越好，因为那是创始人建这东西的原因，对吧？你想用 Duolingo 或 Grammarly 或 Chess.com 改善教育，这些是 meant to be 广铺的产品、有很广的价值主张、全球适用。所以显然，最低摩擦就是免费产品。所以光那是其中一部分。另一部分是很多这类产品主要通过口碑增长，尤其如果你能在产品里建网络效应，像 Duolingo 有一堆社交功能，或者 Grammarly 也有点 B2C2B 的玩法。所以你看到 Grammarly 被团队和公司用，即使用户在免费计划，他们仍在确保 Grammarly 能被同事或团队成员买上提供相当多价值。所以我觉得这些通常是为什么我倾向确保你给用户的核心价值主张是免费、且永久免费，然后你在上面叠一层某些高级功能的尝鲜或样本。那通常是我看到的甜区。关于试用、反向试用那种，我觉得大多看情况。我觉得如果你有个尤其 B2B 的功能、可能有些锁定，反向试用可以超有力。你只想让人进来。你不需要要他们信用卡，因为他们用你的 CRM 或他们在建材料和内容投了相当多时间。所以当那个窗口掉下，你其实感觉「哦哥们，我可能应……」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me follow this thread of just consumer subscription products. I feel like this is the category that every indie developer dreams of building a product in because it's easy to build. Cool, I'll build an app, I add a paywall, and then they realize this is a lot harder than I thought. From a perspective of distribution and CAx and growth like that, is that the biggest missing piece that people don't get about building a successful consumer subscription product?
turns.zh: 让我跟这个消费订阅产品的线。我觉得这是每个独立开发者dream建产品的类别，因为容易建。酷，我建个 app，我加个付费墙，然后他们意识到这比想的难多了。从分发和 CAC 和增长的角度，那是人们关于打造成功消费订阅产品最大的认知缺失吗？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, user retention is gold for consumer subscription companies. If you don't retain your users, then a lot of the onus is on getting them to pay on day one, that's super hard. Then you're dealing with totally different business models where you're paying for users, you're trying to aggressively upsell them before they hit any habitual usage patterns with your product. (00:28:53): A lot of apps naturally do that because that's how they break the mold and get their first users to do it, but I don't know, I've been fortunate to join companies after that initial phase, but especially take Duolingo and Chess.com, these are organic word of mouth driven businesses and in both ways, they grew the market from a much smaller market and as opposed to it being a very competitive space where you're competing and taking market share from others and bidding for higher terms and stuff like that. So I don't know, there's something to that.
turns.zh: 对，用户留存对消费订阅公司是金子。如果你留不住用户，那很多压力在首日让他们付费，那超难。然后你处理完全不同的商业模式——你为用户付费、你在他们跟产品形成任何习惯用法之前就激进 upsell。很多 app 自然那么做，因为那是他们打破模、拿到第一批用户的方式，但我不知道，我很幸运在初始阶段之后加入这些公司，但尤其拿 Duolingo 和 Chess.com，这些是有机口碑驱动的业务，而且两种方式，它们把市场从一个小得多的市场长大，而不是一个你跟人竞争、从别人那抢份额、竞更高价的超竞争空间。所以我不知道，那有点道理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing here is you need to find a way to grow through word of mouth for this to have any chance of success and also retention needs to be very high. Do you have a heuristic of what retention needs to be for you to have a chance building a successful consumer subscription business?
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是，你需要找到一种通过口碑增长的方式、这才有任何成功机会，而且留存需要很高。你有关于留存需要多高的启发式、才能有机会建成功消费订阅业务吗？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: I think consumer companies tend to track essentially two main types of user retention. There's more of the new user, one, D1, D7, et cetera. I think when you have your D one retention somewhere around the 30 or 40% mark, that's quite solid I think for a consumer app. If it's much lower than that, then sometimes I might question the intent of the user or the ability for that, you to I guess acquire just mathematically acquire enough users such that you can grow a big enough daily active user base.
turns.zh: 我觉得消费公司倾向追踪基本两类用户留存。一类是更多新用户的，D1、D7 等等。我觉得当你的 D1 留存大概在 30 或 40% 标记，那对消费 app 相当扎实，我想。如果比那低很多，那有时我可能质疑用户的意图、或者你——我猜数学上——获取足够用户从而长大到足够大的日活基数的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's surprisingly low.
turns.zh: 那意外地低。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it feels achievable in theory.
turns.zh: 所以理论上感觉可达。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: It's achievable. It's achievable in theory, but there are so many options out there in the market and people are feeling a lot of app and product bloat.
turns.zh: 可达。理论上可达，但市场上有这么多选项、人们感觉很多 app 和产品臃肿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so just to be clear, you're saying 20 to 30% of people come back the next day?
turns.zh: 所以要清楚，你说的是 20 到 30% 的人第二天回来？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, 30 to 40.

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: 40%. I think you're an okay place. I think even more importantly, and you mentioned Jorge to kick this off, but he wrote that very, very popular article about the growth model and how current user retention rate was the biggest thing for them. And I think especially if you have a product that has daily frequency, that's actually the retention that matters the most is that of your existing user base that has developed a habitual pattern, how sticky is your product? And it's that retention rate that really compounds and builds that daily habit. (00:31:04): So over time, especially when companies mature a little bit, you actually focus most of your energy on the existing user retention mechanics. You find that that's a much, much bigger lever. One exception is that Grammarly was a different type of product and that you install it and you don't proactively open it every day. So that was interesting to me because I assumed that you should always just focus on existing user retention, but for a product like Grammarly, it's actually the activation installation aha moment that's really, really critical and will carry the user for a very, very long time.
turns.zh: 40%。我觉得你在一个 okay 的地方。我觉得甚至更重要的是，你用 Jorge 开了这个头，但他写了那篇非常非常火的关于增长模型的文章，说当前用户留存率对他们是最重要的事。而且我觉得尤其如果你有个每天频度的产品，其实最重要的留存是那些已经形成习惯模式的现有用户基——你的产品多粘？而那留存率才真正复利、建起那个日常习惯。所以随时间，尤其公司成熟一点，你其实把大部分精力放在现有用户留存机制上。你发现那是大得多的杠杆。一个例外是 Grammarly 是不同类型的产品——你装上它、你不每天主动开它。所以那对我有趣，因为我假设你应该总聚焦现有用户留存，但对 Grammarly 这种产品，其实激活安装那个 aha 时刻才真正关键、会 carry 用户非常非常久。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. Yeah, the stats would show someone's a daily active user because they're typing things and that's not an accurate step for Grammarly. The other interesting trend I've noticed across successful consumer subscription products is they always start very scrappy and very cost-efficient and spend efficient because I think it's because it takes them a long time to find something that's working and they're surviving on that margin of retention to growth cost essentially.
turns.zh: 那说得通。对，数据会显示某人是日活，因为他们打字，而对 Grammarly 那不是个准确步骤。我注意到的另一个成功消费订阅产品的有趣趋势是，它们总起步很 scrappy、很省成本、花得高效，因为我觉得因为它们要花很久找管用的东西、而且它们基本靠那个「留存对增长成本」的余量活着。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, that's right.
turns.zh: 对，那是对的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and the retention piece, that's such a good point. My newsletter is very much along these lines. It's just like how many people are joining every day, how many people are leaving? And it's a difficult treadmill to be on because people, they want to save money, they want to spend on Netflix and things like that. So as amazing as you are, people are always going to leave. So the trick is how do you find more people coming than going?
turns.zh: 对，留存这块，那好点。我的 Newsletter 就很沿这些线。就是每天多少人加入、多少人离开？而那是个难上的跑步机，因为人们想省钱、想花在 Netflix 那些。所以不管你多厉害，人们总会走。所以窍门是怎么找更多进来的人比走的。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, and I think just to take Chess.com example, I think probably 80% of our daily or weekly active users, I'll check the numbers, but something like that would be a current user or an existing user and then a new and a reactivated or resurrected user. Those are actually about similar size for a company of our sale. So even though there's a lot of attention on that new user experience, it's actually pretty interesting that the components of your active user base are actually not heavily weighed in the new user set after you mature to a certain degree.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得就拿 Chess.com 举例，我觉得大概 80% 我们的日或周活用户——我会查数字——但类似那样会是当前用户或现有用户、然后一个新用户和一个重新激活或复活的用户。对那些对我们规模的公司其实大小类似。所以即使对新用户体验有很多关注，有趣的是你活跃用户基的组成部分其实在成熟到一定程度后，不重在新用户集。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you explain that a little bit more?
turns.zh: 你能再解释一点吗？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yes. So after some period of time, you stack up a lot of inactive users in your product and you also stack up sporadic users, people that may not have a daily habit, but they will use it once or twice a week or once or twice a month type of thing. And so eventually that math adds up where you have, let's say hundreds of millions of dormant users that are coming back and it's actually worth spending some time making sure that that resurrected, for lack of a better word, experience inside the product is really excellent and that you find novel ways to try to bring them back. (00:33:38): Duolingo as an example, they did a good job of using social notifications. And so if people would use contact sync or something, you might get a push notification that one of your best friends just started using Duolingo and that might encourage you to come back and resurrect into the product. And whether you resurrected in the product, it might be the case that your proficiency of the language you were learning, you were learning French three years ago, but now you for forgot most of it. And so when you open the app again, it encourages you to essentially replace yourself, do another placement test and put you in the right spot. And so some of these types of mechanics for a more mature company can lead to pretty good ROI guess is what I'm trying to say.
turns.zh: 能。所以过一段时间后，你在产品里堆了很多不活跃用户、也堆了零星用户——那些可能没有每天习惯、但一周一两次或一月一两次用的人。所以最终那数学加起来，你有，比如几亿休眠用户回来，而其实值得花点时间确保那个复活——姑且这么说——在产品内的体验真出色、而且你找新颖方式试着把他们带回来。Duolingo 举例，他们用社交通知做得好。所以如果人们用联系人同步之类，你可能收到推送说你一个最好的朋友刚开始用 Duolingo，那可能鼓励你回来、在产品里复活。而无论你在产品里复活没，可能是你学的语言熟练度——你三年前学法语，但现在忘大部分了。所以当你再开 app，它鼓励你基本 replace 自己、做另一个分级测试、把你放对位置。所以某些这类机制对更成熟的公司能带来相当好 ROI，这是我想说的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Essentially, so many people have already tried in the past that to grow, you need to resurrect people that have been there. And so thinking through, it's almost like a user experience for resurrected users.
turns.zh: 懂了。Basically，这么多人过去试过，所以要增长，你需要复活那些去过的人。所以想清楚，那几乎是给复活用户的用户体验。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let's zoom out a little bit. You've worked at three of the most successful consumer subscription products in the world. What is the difference between how these three operate? I think there's many ways to be successful. It feels like these companies are very different. What's the gist of each of these, how they operate?
turns.zh: 好。让我们 zoom out 一点。你在全球最成功的三个消费订阅产品工作过。这三家运作方式有什么不同？我觉得有很多方式能成功。这些公司感觉很不同。每家的要点、它们怎么运作？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Well, first of all, there's obviously a lot of similarities, but I'll just focus my answer on the differences. So I think Duolingo, what struck me most working there is they're very particular, they have an approach of product development that is infused across everyone in the company. And they actually wrote a playbook about this. It's called the Green Machine if you look it up. That was one of my most successful tweets ever really.
turns.zh: 好，首先 obviously 有很多相似，但我就聚焦我答案在差异。所以我觉得 Duolingo，最打动我的是他们非常特别，他们有种产品开发方式 infused 全公司每个人。他们其实写了本关于这个的 playbook。叫 Green Machine，如果你查。那其实是我最成功的推文之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I just tweeted something about Duolingo just released their playbook and I screenshotted the owl's butt and screened like a page and it was like 5,000 likes.
turns.zh: 我刚发了条关于 Duolingo 刚发了他们 playbook、我截了猫头鹰的屁股、截了像一页、然后五千赞。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: That's hilarious.
turns.zh: 那太好笑了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So yeah, keep going. Sorry.
turns.zh: 对。所以，继续。抱歉。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: But yeah, the ethos of the company. They hire a lot of intelligent, energetic people out of college basically, and they give them a lot of amazing experimentation, tooling, and they care a lot about the clock speed of the company. So it's a lot of creativity, a lot of ideation. (00:35:46): The product experience of dual legal actually changes multiple times per day for each user, which is pretty shocking. And so I'd never worked in a place like that before, but it really struck me about how consistently the company operated and they had specs and processes for doing each of those steps in their product development cycle and they were really, really tight about it.
turns.zh: 但对，公司的 ethos。他们基本从大学招很多聪明、有能量的人，给他们很多超棒的实验、工具，而且他们很在乎公司的 clock speed。所以是很多创意、很多构思。Duolingo 的产品体验其实每个用户一天变多次，挺 shocking。而我之前从没在那种地方工作过，但它真让我震惊于公司运作多一致、他们对产品开发周期每一步都有 spec 和流程、而且真的真的 tight。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so that's still lingo.
turns.zh: 好，所以那还是 lingo。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, that's still lingo. Grammarly. This is an interesting company because they started as a paid product oriented at students. Then they expanded into more of a freemium model tailored to everyone gradually focusing more on the professional base. And then as they accumulate a lot more professionals, they realize, "Hey, there's patterns." We're seeing that a bunch of marketing teams or a bunch of sales teams or a bunch of customer support teams or whatever, particular functions within particular companies were really adopting Grammarly at scale. (00:36:41): And so they were able to then layer on much more of a managed enterprisey motion. And while I was there, I was focused on the consumer self-serve motion, but they weren't siloed. They were intermixed with each other. And so a big part of my job was not just to grow the self-serve revenue and self-serve active users, but it was also how do you uncover the right teams, the right functions, the right companies for demand gen and sales to go reach out to? (00:37:12): So that was a very interesting, it's a product-led sales work, and it's really fascinating thing for me to learn. And then on top of that, with all the transformation going on with generative AI, and even recently with them acquiring CODA and Superhuman and becoming more of a productivity suite, the company is just evolving pretty rapidly. It's a really exciting thing for me to be a part of and to see from the sidelines, but that just made it at its core of a different growth job than Duolingo for sure.
turns.zh: 对，那还是 lingo。Grammarly。这是个有趣公司，因为他们从面向学生的付费产品起步。然后他们扩成更 freemium、 tailored 给每个人、逐渐更聚焦专业基。然后随他们积累更多专业人士，他们意识到「嘿，有模式。」我们看到一堆营销团队或销售团队或客服团队，特定公司里的特定职能真的在规模采用 Grammarly。所以他们能然后叠上多很多的托管企业化动作。而我在那的时候，我聚焦消费者自助动作，但他们不筒仓。他们互相交织。所以我工作很大一部分不只是长自助收入和自助活跃用户，还有怎么揭开对的团队、对的职能、对的公司给需求生成和销售去触达？那是非常有趣的、是产品驱动销售的工作，对我是个真 fascinating 的事去学。然后上面，所有生成式 AI 的转型，甚至最近他们收购 Coda 和 Superhuman、变得更像生产力套件，公司就在很快演化。对我是个超兴奋的事去参与、从旁看，但那让它核心是个不同的增长活，比 Duolingo 肯定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Essentially a B2B business versus a very consumer business?
turns.zh: Basically 一个 B2B 业务 vs 一个非常消费的业务？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, and a lot more meaningful strategic decisions as well.
turns.zh: 对，而且多很多有意义的战略决定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯哼。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: And then the core product team also, I'm used to in growth, laying out the entire user journey that a user go through acquisition, activation, engagement, so on and so forth. And typically, growth teams, if they're well-resourced, they can do enough to move each one of these various levers. And it's just a matter of the sequencing of them and what you want to prioritize first. But Grammarly was unique in that the core product experience itself was what drove repeated activity. (00:38:18): It's that I previously mentioned that current user retention thing, what most drives that is the frequency and the quality of the suggestions that you get every day. And so it was an interesting learning in that I staffed up a growth team, tried to work on this metric, and then I realized actually I'm just getting in the way. This is really a thing that the core product team most influences. Let me have a conversation with the core product leader and then shift that over to them. And so through the neural network, it just gets smarter every time. And because it can have that repetition times a billion or a trillion, I don't know exactly what number, but it's going to get pretty damn good.
turns.zh: 对。我的理解是那个，那个纪录片 incredible，顺便。我不知道你看过 AlphaGo 没，他们把这么技术深的东西做得这么情绪化和人性，惊人。但我觉得那是我们对 AI 和建的产品感觉的 crux，其实。但对你点，我的理解是 AlphaZero 主要训练方式是它就跟自己下 bunch 游戏。所以通过神经网络，它每次变聪明。而因为它能有那重复乘十亿或万亿，我不知道确切数，但会变得相当 damn 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let's go back on track to where we were going. So this was how AI is impacting chess.com. How is AI changing just the work of a growth person?
turns.zh: 好。让我们回轨道到我们要去的。所以这是 AI 怎么影响 chess.com。AI 怎么就改变增长人的工作？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: I like to describe growth as the job is to connect users to the value of your product. And in order to do that, what I like to do is think about that user journey again, and essentially, staff teams that are oriented around each element of that user journey. And those teams have specific metric goals, they have roadmaps, et cetera. And then they go run against them. (00:51:52): So that's how it's structured. AI, I think can be applied to speed up some elements of that essentially experiment cycle that you get through. So one example is in product discovery. As opposed to core product, which tends to have longer timeframes, and you might do thorough user research or market research. It's more foundational, more for first principles, et cetera. Growth is a little bit less like that. (00:52:18): It's like you're running a lot of experiments and the output of any given experiment is the input to your next idea. And so historically, I don't even mean historically, but just a few months ago, we were operating in a, that's history, I suppose, but there would be a lot of manual writing of these analysis docs. You'd have to read them, you'd have to understand what insight you want to grab from them and then write another spec to translate that idea. That's still happening to some degree, but I think that's a spot where even tools like ChatGPT are super helpful. (00:52:56): You can just plug in like an analysis that another person wrote and just have it summarized for you and give you advice on ideas to go try. And so that ideation, that research cycle was much, much faster. I talked a little bit about prototyping also just becoming much, much faster than before. We have not yet gotten to the point where product managers themselves are actually shipping the code into production, but it's dramatically shortened the amount of time it takes to conceive of especially a bolder idea that you might have. (00:53:27): And so when I talked earlier about explore and exploit, a lot of the explore was harder to do, but now it's a little bit easier to do. You can take a broader concept and visualize it, and when you can visualize it, send it around the team, get people to click around it, that makes a world of difference. So those are just a couple examples that come to mind.
turns.zh: 我喜欢把增长描述成：工作是把用户连到你产品的价值。而为了做那个，我喜欢做的是再想那个用户旅程，basic，staff 围绕那个用户旅程每个元素的团队。而那些团队有具体指标目标、有路线图等等。然后他们去跑那些。所以那是它结构化的方式。AI，我觉得能被 apply 去加速那个实验循环的某些元素、你过的。所以一个例子在产品发现。相对于核心产品——往往有更长 timeframe、你可能做彻底用户研究或市场研究，更基础、更第一性原理——增长有点不那么像那样。它像你跑很多实验、任何给定实验的输出是你下一个想法的输入。而历史上，我不 even 指历史上，就几个月前，我们在运作一个，那历史了，我想，但会有很多手动写这些分析 doc。你得读它们、你得理解你想从它们抓什么洞察、然后写另一个 spec 去翻译那个想法。那还在发生某种程度，但我觉得那是个 spot 即使 ChatGPT 这种工具也超有帮助。你就能塞进像别人写的分析、让它给你总结、给你该试的想法的建议。所以那构思、那研究循环快多得多。我也聊了点原型也变快多得多。我们还没到 PM 自己把代码 ship 进生产的程度，但它戏剧性缩短了构思尤其一个你可能有的更大胆想法的时间。所以我早聊探索与利用时，很多……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I want to go back to this phrase right at the beginning of this answer that you shared that I think is really helpful that you see growth as simply your job is to connect users to the value of your product.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我想回你这答案开头分享的那句话，我觉得真有帮助——你把增长看成 simply 你的工作是把用户连到你产品的价值。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you speak more to that? Because I think that's such a nice way clarifying what is growth's role?
turns.zh: 你能多讲那个吗？因为我觉得那是澄清增长角色是什么的这么好的方式？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, it resonates deeply with me because I feel like growth sometimes gets this reputation I guess that it's just pure metrics hacking, like we're cold people that just are trying to move a particular metric up and we're going to do whatever it can to throw walls and pay walls and add friction in all these spots. And even though that could theoretically work at a micro level on a specific feature or a specific metric, I think what's most healthy for a company, and I want to work at durable companies is to think about the user holistically. (00:54:42): And when you take that framing of connecting users to the value of your product, that value can change for a user over time, and that also lines up really nicely to the journey. What someone that's not even a user yet needs to understand about the value proposition is super different than what a habitual user of three plus years might need. And so the teams working on them should think from that perspective and then from there, then ladder into specific problems to solve hypotheses, et cetera.
turns.zh: 对，它 deep 共鸣我，因为我觉得增长有时得到这种名声——我想——它只是纯指标黑客，像我们冷的人就试着把一个特定指标弄上去、我们会做任何能做的去扔墙和付费墙、加摩擦在所有这些点。而即使那理论上能在微观层、在特定功能或特定指标 work，我觉得对公司最健康、而我想在耐久公司工作的是想用户 holistically。当你拿那个框架——连用户到你产品的价值——那价值对用户随时间变，而且那也漂亮地排到旅程。一个甚至还不是用户的人需要理解的关于价值主张，跟一个三年加习惯用户需要的 super 不同。所以那些团队该从那视角想、然后从那 ladder 进具体问题去解假设等等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Following that thread a little bit more, people listening to this are imagining, "How do I get better at experimentation? How do I run more experiments? How do we do this better?" What are two or three tips and best practices that you think people need to hear maybe are not totally aware of when they think about getting better at experimentation on our teams?
turns.zh: 跟那线多一点，听的人在想象「我怎么在实验上变好？我怎么跑更多实验？我们怎么把这做得更好？」你觉得人们需要听到、也许当他们想团队实验变好时没完全意识到的两三个 tips 和最佳实践是什么？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: I think the first thing is just start somewhere. I just read this Atlassian state of product report and it was like 40% of product teams basically don't run experimentation at all. And there may be some good reasons for it. It could be philosophical or maybe you're more B2B oriented or whatever. So I get it, but I think for a lot of, especially if you work on a consumer product that has some degree of scale, some degree of frequency with your product, you can collect enough data. (00:56:05): And also I have found I can pattern match all day long. I've worked a lot of companies, right? But I'm wrong all the time. And I think consumer behavior can be very fickle and especially when you work at a company, you become a power user naturally. So sometimes you may forget what the actual user experience is for a brand new user, and so you leave a lot of opportunities on the table if you don't even try to experiment. (00:56:27): So I just encourage taking that first step, just run an A/B test, find a third-party tool or something that you can integrate quickly or even just work with your engineers to spin something up. Just get in the practice of crawl then walk then run type of thing.
turns.zh: 我觉得第一是就从哪里开始。我刚读 Atlassian 的产品状态报告，像 40% 产品团队 basic 根本不跑实验。而可能有好理由。可能哲学上、或你更 B2B 导向或啥。所以我懂，但我觉得对很多、尤其如果你在有个某种规模、某种频度的消费产品，你能收足够数据。而且我也发现我能 pattern match 一整天。我工作很多公司，对吧？但我一直错。而我觉得消费行为能很 fickle、尤其当你在公司工作，你自然变超级用户。所以有时你可能忘了一个全新用户的真实体验是什么，所以如果你甚至不试实验，你留很多机会在桌上。所以我 just 鼓励迈那第一步，就跑个 A/B 测、找个第三方工具或你能快集成的、或甚至跟工程师搞个。就进 crawl 然后 walk 然后 run 那种练习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite tool, by the way? Just to throw out? Is there a go-to tool for you?
turns.zh: 顺便，你有喜欢工具吗？就扔一个？你有 go-to 工具？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: We used Statsig at Grammarly and I saw that they recently got acquired, so that was exciting news. Duolingo and Chess.com both have an in-house experimentation approach.
turns.zh: 我们在 Grammarly 用 Statsig，我看到他们最近被收购，所以那兴奋新闻。Duolingo 和 Chess.com 都有内部实验方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet.
turns.zh: 甜。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Pros and cons to either. Obviously Duolingo is an experimentation machine, and so it's been a huge accelerant to have our own thing specifically tailored to be excellent at that. But no, I typically don't encourage companies to build experimentation in-house from day one. At a certain scale it can make sense. And some of these companies, they were started 15 years ago when these tools weren't out. So it was just something they had to do.
turns.zh: 各有 pros cons。显然 Duolingo 是个实验机器，所以有我们自己 tailored 超擅长那个的东西是巨大加速。但不，我 typically 不鼓励公司 day one 建实验内部。在某规模它 make sense。而有些公司，他们 15 年前起步时这些工具还没出。所以只是他们得做的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that you mentioned to me at Chess.com, your goal is to run a thousand experiments a year. You said you were at 250. Talk about just that as a North Star.
turns.zh: 你在 Chess.com 提过，你的目标是一年跑一千个实验。你说你在 250。讲讲那个作为北极星。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, so part of having team members that are fanatical about Chess is that the company can get pretty far just building for themselves, building for the community, and not actually being very experimentation and data oriented. The problem with that is that you can have relatively lumpy growth. And so part of the excitement of me joining the company was to help smooth that out and bring in that experimentation mindset. (00:57:56): So prior to 2023, the company practically didn't experiment at all. Last year they did about 50, this year they're on pace for about 250. And then next year we have that ambitious target of a thousand. Did I make it up? Yes, absolutely, I made it up, but it's still a target and a thing for the teams to think about and a thousand experiments by itself. If you just did that but you didn't learn, you didn't make an impact, that's kind of a waste of time. (00:58:25): The whole point of setting a goal is that you can have conversations about what would need to be true to actually hit that goal, and so that leads to insights. Actually we need not just product management or engineering to be running these experiments. We can experiment with lifecycle marketing, changing copy of push notifications and emails. We can experiment with app store screenshots and keywords and stuff like that. We have all sorts of content marketing teams, et cetera. We could have engineering enable no code for specific screens. (00:58:58): Think about our home screen or our pricing screen where we might want to do a lot of just tests that are configurable without engineering support. We might want to just track our progress and look at it from time to time and make sure that we have the right observability around this. So anyway, that's the stuff that really matters as opposed to the hitting that goal itself. So don't tell the team, but I don't actually care that much if we actually hit a thousand, but I think if we get pretty close and we accomplish some of these things, we'll be in really good shape.
turns.zh: 对，所以有 fanatical 关于棋的团队成员的部分是，公司能走相当远就为自己建、为社区建、而其实不很实验和数据导向。那的问题是你能有相对 lump 增长。所以我加入公司的兴奋部分之一是帮平那、带进那实验心态。所以 2023 前，公司 practical 根本不实验。去年他们做约 50，今年他们在 pace 约 250。然后明年我们有那雄心目标一千。我编的吗？对，绝对我编的，但它仍是个目标、团队要想的事、而一千实验本身。如果你 just 做那个但你没学、你没造成影响，那有点浪费时间。设目标的整点是你能有对话关于什么需要为真才能真打到那目标，而那 Lead 到洞察。其实我们需要不只产品管理或工程跑这些实验。我们能跟生命周期营销实验、改推送和邮件的文案。我们能跟应用商店截图和关键词实验那些。我们有各种内容营销团队等等。我们能有工程 enable 无代码给特定屏。想我们主屏或定价屏——我们可能想做很多就 configurable 不用工程支持的测。我们可能只想追进度、时不时看、确保我们有对这的正确可观测性。所以总之，那才是真重要的、相对于打到目标本身。所以别告诉团队，但我其实不 care 那么多我们真打到一千，但我觉得如果我们接近、而且完成一些这些事……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, we'll make sure none of them watch this. I think chess.com is in, this is just such a cool example of a culture shifting dramatically from zero experiments to sounds like two years later, a thousand, which is three a day. There's many teams running experiments in parallel, but that's a lot. What has helped you most shift that culture? Is it just the CEO being like, "This is the way we're going to go." What have you learned about helping shift to culture from No, we're not doing experiments to a thousand experiments a year.
turns.zh: 好，我们确保他们没一个看这个。我觉得 chess.com 在，这是个超酷的文化从零实验戏剧性转到听起来两年后一千、那是每天三个。有很多团队并行跑实验，但那很多。什么帮你最多转那文化？就是 CEO 像「这是我们要走的方式」？你学到什么关于帮转文化从「不，我们不实验」到「一年一千实验」？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, definitely a lot of credit to the CEO and co-founders like Erik and Danny, they're amazing. It's not their intuitive way of thinking about growing companies, but their mental flexibility and encouragement to evolve and add this as a tool for the company has been awesome, and they've been on the front lines preaching product-led growth and experimentation just as much as I have. (01:00:20): So I'm glad that you brought that up because I think that is critically important for me, joining a company to not be at odds with the co-founders and the existing approach of the company. I think that's absolutely, absolutely critical. I think I started this podcast with the example of the game review and the positivity and how that was shared. I think those types of things are really what motivate people. They need to see this working in practice.
turns.zh: 对，绝对很多 credit 给 CEO 和联合创始人像 Erik 和 Danny，他们 amazing。那不是他们直觉想增长公司的方式，但他们的心理灵活性和鼓励演化、加这个作为公司工具超棒，而且他们在前线 preach 产品驱动增长和实验就跟我一样多。所以我 glad 你提那个，因为我觉得对我 critically 重要——加入公司不与联合创始人和公司现有方式对立。我觉得那绝对绝对 critical。我觉得我用这播客以对局复盘和 positivity 的例子开了头、那怎么被分享。我觉得那类事是真 motivate 人的。他们需要看这在实践中 work。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wins.
turns.zh: 胜利。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, you need wins, you got to celebrate them. People feel good about the learning. It's applied across the board. Who's not going to be energized by that, I think, right? So you can't just set goals in a vacuum and create it from top, right? People have to see it working and when it works, the metrics move and you learn faster and you ship faster, and that's a great environment to be part of.
turns.zh: 对，你需要胜利、你得庆祝它们。人对学习感觉好。它应用到 board。谁不会被那 energized，我想，对吧？所以你不能 just 在真空设目标、从顶创建，对吧？人得看它 work、而当它 work，指标动、你学更快、你 ship 更快，而那是个超棒环境去成为部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was the first experiment you guys ran? Do you remember?
turns.zh: 你们跑的第一个实验是什么？你记得吗？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: I don't know, before my time actually.
turns.zh: 我不知道，其实在我来之前。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay. Got it. So they're already going down this track before they brought you in?
turns.zh: 好。好。懂了。所以他们已经在这轨道、在把你招进来前？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: They had run some.
turns.zh: 他们跑了一些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, sweet. Are there any other key lessons that you think people need to know to be successful running experiments at scale?
turns.zh: 好，甜。有别的你觉得人需要知道的关键课来成功大规模跑实验吗？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: The system matters just as much as any given experiment, probably even more, right? I think starting with a growth model, so you have an understanding of how your company grows in the first place and which channels you're going to leverage is critical. You need to make sure that you are instrumenting your product in and out. Otherwise, you're going to run experiments and have wonky results. (01:01:53): I won't name which company, but I was part of a company that had an in-house experimentation tool. It's about three months into the company, we're running some experiments and we realized that user retention was actually configured backwards. So all positive results were negative results.
turns.zh: 系统重要就跟任何给定实验一样多、可能更多，对吧？我觉得从增长模型开始，所以你有理解你公司首先怎么增长、你要 leverage 哪些渠道是 critical。你需要确保你 in 和 out 埋点你的产品。否则你跑实验会有 wonky 结果。我不会点名哪公司，但我曾是一公司有部分内部实验工具。公司约三个月时，我们跑一些实验、我们意识到用户留存其实配反了。所以所有正结果都是负结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Geez.
turns.zh: 天。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: So that was kind of embarrassing and that will never happen again.
turns.zh: 所以那有点尴尬、而那再不会发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You just go through and undo all those experiments and just drive up retention.
turns.zh: 你就过、undo 所有那些实验、就 drive up 留存。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: It's kind of weird. We're seeing people use the features a lot more. Why is user retention going negative? So I have plenty of horror stories around that type of stuff, but yeah.
turns.zh: 有点怪。我们看到人们用功能多得多。为什么用户留存走负？所以我有一堆那种 horror story，但对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God. On the flip side of horror stories, you've shared a bunch of cool examples of experiment wins. Is there another that comes to mind of one you're really proud of or that was really trajectory changing either at Duolingo or Grammarly or Chess?
turns.zh: 哦我的天。在 horror story 反面，你分享了一堆实验胜利酷例子。有另一个想到你真骄傲的、或真改变轨迹的、在 Duolingo 或 Grammarly 或 Chess？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: So I already shared one of Chess.com and one of Grammarly. I could talk a bit about Duolingo as well. Duolingo and you had Jackson on the podcast, right? Where you talked about the streaks.
turns.zh: 所以我已分享一个 Chess.com 和一个 Grammarly。我能聊点 Duolingo。Duolingo 而你有过 Jackson 上播客，对吧？你们聊了 streak。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes, talked about the streaks.
turns.zh: 对，聊了 streak。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: So I also don't want to steal his thunder because I was going to think about that, but the amount of learning through commitment and putting streaks on a calendar and just getting people started as opposed to achieving some large milestone, that was huge. I think we did something interesting. We spun up a virality team and virality is this really amorphous thing to me. (01:03:16): I think it's really hard to generate virality in your product, but Duolingo is a product that is shared quite a bit. And so we invested actually in some time to essentially add screenshot tracking for a brief period of time in the app just so we could find out the hotspots of where users were doing screenshots. And you see this in other apps too, it's not necessarily some horrible thing, but we did this for some period of time and we were able to basically articulate and say, "Okay, streak milestones is the obvious one." (01:03:46): Really funny challenges that you get in the Duolingo experience is also super highly shared. Advancing in the top three of a leaderboard is another thing. Anyway, so you can find these different moments where that's the case. And then we staffed those moments with illustrators and animators and created these really delightful experiences around them, and that worked amazingly well. (01:04:06): So as opposed to going against I guess human intuition and trying to get them to share stuff that they otherwise wouldn't on the margins want to share, lean into it more, actually grab the moments where users are already organically screenshotting and make those much, much, much better. And you can 5X or 10X and drive a lot of growth that way too. So that's not so much an experiment, it's more a core product thing, but it just resonated with me that that was interesting.
turns.zh: 所以我也不想偷他 thunder 因为我要想那个，但通过承诺放 streak 在日历、就让人开始而不是达成某个大里程碑，那学习量巨大。我觉得我们做了有趣事。我们起了个病毒团队、而病毒对我是很 amorphous 东西。我觉得在你产品生病毒很难，但 Duolingo 是个被分享相当多的产品。所以我们其实投了点时间基本加 screenshot 追踪一小段在 app 就为找用户做 screenshot 的热点。你在别 app 也看到，不一定是 horrible 事，但我们做那段时间、我们基本能阐明说「好，streak 里程碑是明显的」。Duolingo 体验里你得的超有趣挑战也被超高分享。在 leaderboard 进前三也是另一件。总之，所以你能找这些不同时刻那是情况。然后我们 staff 那些时刻用插画师和动画师、创这些真 delightful 体验围绕它们，而那 work amazingly 好。所以相对于 against 我猜人类直觉、试让他们分享他们否则不会在边缘想分享的，lean into 它更多、其实抓那些用户已经在有机 screenshot 的时刻、让那些好得多多。而你能 5X 或 10X、那样 drive 很多增长。所以那不那么是个实验，更是核心产品事，但它就共鸣我那有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, it connects to your explore and exploit methodology. Just find or explore where things are happening and then try to exploit in a nice positive way.
turns.zh: 好，它连到你探索与利用方法。就找或探索事在哪发生、然后试以 nice 正面方式利用。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: You got it.
turns.zh: 你懂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of that, you mentioned this with Duolingo is just very good at habit formation and motivation behavior. It feels like chess is good at this too. You've worked at both these companies. What have you learned about how to motivate people? How to create habits?
turns.zh: 说到那，你提过 Duolingo 就非常擅长习惯形成和动机行为。感觉棋也擅长这个。你在这两家都工作过。你学到怎么 motivate 人？怎么创习惯？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Again, Duolingo would not have started without this insight from day one. They aim to focus on motivation and build a lot of these tactics. Jorge actually had this model of gamification patterns having essentially three pillars to it. You have the core loop, you have the metagame, and then you have the profile. And so we actually thought about it that way too, where your core loop is your lesson that you go through. You do a lesson, you get some rewards, you extend your streak, and then the next day you get a push notification. (01:05:29): It's the core loop of the product and making that really tight is super important because people need a habit to stick to. Then you need a metagame, which for Duolingo is the path, but it's also the leaderboard achievements. It's long-term things that you're going to strive to such that you have long-term, I guess, motivation to continue doing the thing. And then the profile is also critical because you build up a profile over time. (01:05:51): It's a reflection of your investment inside the product experience. And so when you nail those three things, you can end up with a long-term learning journey that can be quite successful. And then to flip over to the Chess.com side, what we see is that over 75% of our new users, they classify themselves as like, "I'm completely new to chess." Or, "I'm a beginner." And unfortunately, if you're new to chess and you're a beginner, you're not going to have that fun of a time playing live games, and we see this in the data. It's like less than a third of those users actually win their first game. And when you lose a game, user retention is 10% worse than when you win a game.
turns.zh: 再说，Duolingo 不会没这洞察从第 1 天起步。他们 aim 聚焦动机、建很多这些战术。Jorge 其实有这模型——游戏化模式基本有三支柱。你有核心循环、你有 metagame、然后你有 profile。所以我们其实也那样想——你的核心循环是你过的课。你过课、你得些奖励、你延长 streak、然后第二天你收推送。它是产品的核心循环、让那真的 tight 超重要因为人需要习惯 stick。然后你需要 metagame，对 Duolingo 是路径、但也是 leaderboard 成就。是长期东西你会 strive to 这样你有长期、我猜、动机继续做那事。然后 profile 也 critical 因为你随时间建起 profile。它是你在产品体验里投资的反映。所以当你 nail 那三件事，你能 end up 有个长期学习旅程能相当成功。然后翻到 Chess.com 侧，我们看到超 75% 新用户，他们 classify 自己像「我完全新手」或「我是初学者」。而不幸地，如果你新手、你是初学者，你不会有那 fun 下 live 棋，我们在数据看到。像少于三分之一那些用户真赢他们第一盘。而当你输一盘，用户留存比赢时差 10%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's not so bad, but at scale, that's bad.
turns.zh: 那不 so bad，但大规模，那 bad。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, and it could be worse. That's true. And so typically what a lot of mobile games will do is they'll just create a super simplified version of the game. It's harder for us to do at chess, and so without changing the rules of that, I think that's, I don't know, it's just very eye-opening to me when you're trying to learn something, whether that be language learning or chess or whatever, usually those first steps are fraught with a lot of self-doubt and reinforcement that you're not good at the thing. And so it pays to be very intentional to craft experiences that guide the user around that.
turns.zh: 对，而且可能更糟。那真。所以通常很多手游会做的是就创个超简化版游戏。对我们棋更难做，而不改规则，我觉得那，我不知道，当你试学东西时它 just 很 eye-opening 给我——无论语言学习或棋或啥——通常那些第一步充满很多自我怀疑和 reinforce 你不擅长那事。所以值得非常 intentional 去 craft 体验 guide 用户绕开那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, I can't help but ask, is there anything that helped that along?
turns.zh: 好，我忍不住问，有啥帮了那个吗？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, so something we're experimenting right now is just like purely if you say that you're new to chess, we're going to craft a more delightful learn how to play experience as opposed to dropping into a live game, that's an example. Another is hiding your ratings for the first five times such that you're not seeing your rating plummet. So there's a lot of tips and tricks you can do.
turns.zh: 对，所以我们在实验的现在是就 pure 如果你说你新手，我们要 craft 更 delightful 的「学怎么玩」体验、而不是掉进 live 棋，那是例子。另一个是对前五次藏你的 rating 这样你不看 rating 暴跌。所以有超多 tips 和 tricks 你能做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm just imagining a little guide that's like, "Here's how you win."
turns.zh: 我就在想个小指南像「这是你怎么赢」。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, or play against a coach, play against a friend, play against a bot. There's a bunch of different avenues you could take.
turns.zh: 对，或跟教练下、跟朋友下、跟 bot 下。有一堆不同路径你能走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, what I'd love is play against someone real and here's where you should move. Just like, "Hey, here's we're going to help you win."
turns.zh: 好，我想要的是跟真人下、这是你该走哪。就像「嘿，我们要帮你赢」。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Like a hint in real-time?
turns.zh: 像实时提示？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 对，对，对。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: I don't want to be playing with you then.
turns.zh: 那我就不想跟你下了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let me ask you a couple more questions. One is just zooming out a little bit, what's the most counterintuitive lesson you've learned about building products or building teams across the many companies you've worked at?
turns.zh: 好。让我问你几个更多问题。一是 zoom out 一点，你在很多工作过的公司学到关于建产品或建团队，最反直觉的一课是什么？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, I've talked a lot about products. So maybe I'll flip to the team side for a bit. I think the standard way to hire and build a team is you fill out a JD, it's got a whole bunch of different characteristics that you're looking for. You typically will find a short list of companies that are kind of similar to yours, and then you try to hire for that, right? I think that's the typical default path that a lot of companies take. (01:08:27): And I was really struck by my experience working at some smaller startups or take Duolingo as an example, where over and over and over, I saw some of the highest performers just being people that had very high agency, had that clock speed, had that energy. Yes, they cared about the mission, but they didn't necessarily need to have deep experience on that matter. And in fact, sometimes that experience could be a crutch in certain ways, especially in this world where the grounds are shifting so fast with AI, a lot of your learned habits actually need to be intentionally discarded. (01:09:01): You need to have a beginner's mind on this type of stuff. So I think this is more true than ever, looking for people that respond and move quickly and think just faster and move faster. I think the fastest speed of learning, those types of companies are the ones that I want to bet on. I think those will end up surviving and thriving.
turns.zh: 对，我聊了很多产品。所以也许我翻到团队侧一阵。我觉得标准招人和建团队方式是你填个 JD，有一堆你在找的不同特征。你典型会找类似你的一小串公司，然后试为那个招，对吧？我觉得那是很多公司走的典型默认路径。而我被我在一些小初创、或拿 Duolingo 当例子时的经验真 struck——一遍又一遍，我看到一些最高绩效的人，就是那些有很高主动性、有那种 clock speed、有那种能量的人。对，他们在乎使命，但他们不一定需要在那件事上有深经验。而其实有时那经验能在某些方面是拐杖，尤其在这个 AI 让地基飞速移动的世界，你很多学来的习惯其实需要被有意丢弃。你需要在这类事上有初学者心态。所以我觉得这比 ever 更真——找那些回应快、动得快、想得更快、动得更快的人。我觉得学习速度最快的那些公司，是我愿意下注的。我觉得那些最终会存活并 thrive。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So just to double click on this idea of high agency is very trending these days of just higher high agency people. To unpack that a little bit, you mentioned a few of these traits, so let's just help people see what you see. So one is clock speed, just they think fast, they move fast, they learn fast. What else? What else do you look for that helps you see that there are high agency people?
turns.zh: 所以就双击这「高主动性」的想法——现在很 trending 招高主动性的人。拆开一点，你提了几个这些特质，所以帮人看到你看到的。一是 clock speed，就他们想得快、动得快、学得快。还有啥？你还看什么帮你识别那是高主动性的人？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, a lot of it actually happens outside of the interview process interestingly. So a lot of it is the types of questions they asked, "Have they actually tried your product and gone deep into it?" A lot of it is, it's the references, it's the communication that they have to even set up your interview, it's the energy they bring into the conversation. (01:10:09): You can actually pick up a lot of soft signals on some of these traits over time. You've got to pick up on some of these patterns. I don't know that I'm perfect at it, but I've learned to balance those things quite a bit more than I did in the past when I would just purely read from my questions and my rubric and not care about anything else.
turns.zh: 对，很多其实发生在面试流程之外，有趣地。所以很多是他们问的问题类型——「他们真试过你的产品、并深进去了吗？」很多是推荐信、是他们为安排你面试的沟通、是他们带进对话的能量。你其实能随时间捡到很多这些特质的软信号。你得 pick up 一些这些模式。我不知道我是否完美，但我学到比过去平衡那些多得多——过去我只纯从我的问题和 rubric 读、不 care 别的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, there's like a vibes component to it. This is also support for the work trial way of interviewing versus just a talk interview where you have them actually work with you for a week or whatever.
turns.zh: 对，有个 vibes 成分。这也支持「工作试用」面试方式、而不是就聊聊——你让他们真跟你工作一周或啥。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: That's a great point.
turns.zh: 好点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. One other question I wanted to ask you. You've worked at a bunch of different sizes of companies from startup to Grammarly, I don't know, you call it a big company, bigger company. Duolingo, I don't know how big is Duolingo?
turns.zh: 好。我想问的另一个。你在不同规模的公司工作过——从初创到 Grammarly，我不知道你叫它大公司、更大的公司。Duolingo，我不知道 Duolingo 多大？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: There are about a thousand people.
turns.zh: 大概一千人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool.
turns.zh: 好，酷。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: But I worked at Google too to start my career.
turns.zh: 但我职业生涯起步也在 Google 工作过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, right, okay. What have you learned about just the size of company that makes you happy? What have you learned about just helping other people that you talk to decide what size of company is good for them?
turns.zh: 哦对，好。你学到关于「公司规模」的什么让你开心？你学到怎么帮别的你聊的人决定什么规模公司对他们好？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: I definitely believe that everyone has a company stage that they shine best at. I've personally gone through this journey of big tech to tiny, tiny, tiny startup, then landed in the middle, which I consider my own goal lock zone. I talked earlier about what actually gives me personally a lot of energy is seeing across a company's efforts, but also the company being small enough that I can get into the details, I can work with the specific teams. (01:11:33): I can read experiment results, I can look at the pixels. And so I find that the balance of those two things tends to fit best with medium-sized companies, but that's me, right? I think at big companies like a Google, you're dealing with immense scale, which is interesting by itself. You learn a lot of best practices from your peers. They have all the tools and functions that you would possibly want to go learn from, but they can tend to move slower and it's harder to ship things and get them out the door, which eventually drove me nuts a little bit. (01:12:06): On the flip end of the spectrum, these tiny startups, they move incredibly fast, but I grew all my gray hair from those tiny startups because no one knows about your company, and so you're recruiting people one by one. You're trying to get users one by one. So yeah, you can learn fast and ship a lot of things, but if you're trying to make a big impact on the world, it can be actually pretty grueling to do so at really, really, really small startups. (01:12:29): Now, some of them do hyperscale and make it out, and obviously, I am not one to trash that because the path that I tried for quite a while. But for me, I really like the zone where I can contribute at scale, but also execute at a pace that's more on the daily and weekly scale as opposed to monthly and quarterly.
turns.zh: 我绝对相信每个人都有个他们最 shine 的公司阶段。我个人走过这旅程——大科技到 tiny tiny tiny 初创，然后落在中间，那是我自己的 goal lock zone。我早聊了什么真给我个人很多能量：是看跨公司的努力，但公司也小到我能进细节、能跟特定团队工作。我能读实验结果、我能看像素。所以我觉得那两件事的平衡 tend 最适合中型公司，但那是我，对吧？我觉得大公司像 Google，你处理巨大规模，本身有趣。你从同侪学很多最佳实践。他们有所有你可能想学的工具和功能，但他们 tend 动更慢、把东西 ship 出门更难，那最终让我有点 nuts。频谱另一端，这些 tiny 初创，他们动难以置信地快，但我所有白头发都从那些 tiny 初创来，因为没人知道你的公司，所以你一个一个招人。你一个一个试拿用户。所以对，你能学快、ship 很多东西，但如果你想对世界造大影响，在真真真小的初创其实可能相当 grueling。现在有些 hyperscale 冲出来，而 obviously 我不是 trush 那个，因为那路径我试了相当久。但对我，我真爱那个 zone——我能规模贡献、但也以日周 pace 执行、而不是月季。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And when you say medium, what size of company is that roughly?
turns.zh: 而你说中型，那大概是什么规模的公司？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: Yeah, so these companies that we've talked about in the podcast are about 500 to a thousand people. Typically, these companies who have been around let's say 10 to 20 years. They're durable, ideally profitable, have a good leadership team, but there's still a lot of dimensions to go figure out. A lot of them are in key inflection points, so they're certainly not stagnant. You need to find a place that's dynamic too.
turns.zh: 对，所以我们播客聊的这些公司大概 500 到一千人。典型这些公司存在了说 10 到 20 年。他们耐久、理想盈利、有好领导团队，但仍有好多维度要搞清。很多在关键 inflection 点，所以他们 certainly 不 stagnant。你需要找也动态的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting, 10 to 20 years old, I don't know if that's a, not many people would feel like that's where I want to be. I love that you found a number of companies like that that you enjoyed working at. The last question, and this is going to be taking us to a recurring segment on the podcast that I call Failed Corner. (01:13:35): People hear all these stories of all these experiments and all these companies that worked at, they're all killing it up into the right. In reality, you've touched on this, a lot of things don't work out great. So can you share a story when something went wrong, when you failed and what that taught you?
turns.zh: 有趣，10 到 20 岁，我不知道那是不是——没多少人会觉得那是我想去的地方。我爱你找到一些那样的公司、你 enjoy 工作。最后一个问题，这会带我们到播客一个 recurring 段落，我叫它「失败角」（Failed Corner）。人们听所有这些实验、所有这些公司的故事、他们全在右上 killing it。现实，你 touch 过这个，很多事不 work out great。所以你能分享一个故事——当某事错了、当你 fail、以及那教你什么？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: First of all, in the growth world, you're failing all the time. So I'm not going to pick a specific growth story because those don't actually hit my ego too much. But earlier in my career I did a lot of core product work. I worked for this startup called Chariot. I don't know if you ever lived in San Francisco, but.
turns.zh: 首先，在增长世界，你一直 fail。所以我不挑个特定增长故事，因为那些其实不 hit 我 ego 太多。但我职业生涯早做很多核心产品工作。我为个叫 Chariot 的初创工作。我不知道你住过旧金山没，但。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes, it was like the bus super thing.
turns.zh: 对，像那个公交 super 东西。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: The blue commuter shuttles, like 15-person shuttles, they would essentially drive from various neighborhoods into downtown San Francisco. It's a commuting use case across between the public bus system and an Uber and Lyft. So I was there for some time. I led product there and the core service was really loved by its users. It was reliable and fast and affordable enough, but we got pretty interested in this idea that maybe we can improve utilization, maybe we can make the service a little bit more innovative if we offer dynamic routes more similar to Uber and Lyft. (01:14:46): How could the drivers are driving these fixed routes? But if they have spare time, they can go out of their way, go pick up somebody at their house or something and keep going. So we tried this, we called the chair direct, really interesting attempt, but I learned a lot of lessons there because ultimately it didn't work out. One lesson is like this was kind of a solution searching for a problem. You never just purely want to chase A, it wouldn't it be nice if we did this as opposed to this is our user and this is the problem that we're solving, this is why it's going to delight them, et cetera, that's one. (01:15:20): Second is you got to consider, especially in these more marketplace type businesses, there's more than just one end user and we focus so much of our attention on the writer app without realizing, oh yeah, the drivers are carrying a lot of the brunt of this experience and our operations team is as well. And so when the drivers are confused or disgruntled, that can lead to a challenging overall experience for the product. So that's definitely another one. (01:15:50): And the third one is we did a lot of actually PR, prior to the service going out just to get the word out. And PR has its time in place, but I think doing it before you have validation that customers definitely want, the thing is quite risky and it can lead to a lot of sun cost once you get it out because you need to see it through, you want to see it succeed. So yeah, this is a decade ago, honestly, I had a great time at that company, but I still remember that vividly because it contained three or more key lessons that carried forward as I have built many products since then.
turns.zh: 蓝色通勤班车，像 15 人班车，他们 basic 从各社区开进旧金山市中心。是个通勤用例——在公交系统和 Uber、Lyft 之间。所以我在那待一阵。我在那 led 产品，核心服务真被用户爱。它可靠、快、够便宜，但我们变得对这想法相当有兴趣——也许我们能改善利用率、也许我们能让服务更创新、如果我们提供动态路线更类似 Uber 和 Lyft。司机开这些固定路线？但如果他们有空时间，他们能绕路、去某人家里接人或啥、继续走。所以我们试这个，我们叫 chair direct，真有趣的尝试，但我在那学很多课，因为最终它没 work out。一课是这有点像 solution searching for a problem。你从不要纯追 A——「如果我们做这个 not 会 nice 吗」——而不是「这是我们的用户、这是我们在解的问题、这是为什么它会 delight 他们」等等，那是一。第二是你得考虑，尤其这些更 marketplace 型业务，不止一个终端用户、我们 focus 这么多注意力在 rider app 没意识到——哦对，司机扛了这体验很多重、我们的运营团队也是。所以当司机困惑或不满，那能 lead 到挑战性的整体体验。所以那绝对是另一个。第三是我们做很多其实 PR，在服务出去前就为传开。而 PR 有它时间和地方，但我觉得在做之前你没验证客户 definite 想要，那事相当 risky、而且一旦出去能 lead 很多 sun cost 因为你需要……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it feels like you went to the complete other end run experiments of everything before you tell anyone about it.
turns.zh: 对，感觉你走到完全另一端——在告任何人前跑一切实验。

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I remember the chariot bus showing up at the Airbnb office and people getting, I'm like, "What the hell is this?"
turns.zh: 对，我记得 chariot 巴士出现在 Airbnb 办公室、人们 get，我像「这啥鬼？」

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very cool. I didn't know you worked there. Albert, we've covered so much ground everything I was hoping we'd cover. Is there anything else that you wanted to cover, anything else you want to leave listeners with before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 超酷。我不知道你在那工作。Albert，我们覆盖了这么多我想覆盖的。有别的你想覆盖的、在进超兴奋的闪电轮前你想留听众什么吗？

turns.speaker: Albert Cheng
turns.en: No, this is great. I hope it was useful for your listeners. I will say over the last few days, as I was prepping for this, I was honestly a little bit anxious about do I have enough deep independent frameworks that I need to come up with? But just being authentic to my actual experience at these companies, a lot of my lessons learned have been off of the backs of other people that have tried similar things and have succeeded or failed. (01:17:21): And I think what's important is that you have that your mental sponge. You can try a bunch of different things, you can absorb them and then put them in practice right away, discard the things that don't work and evolve them for yourself and for the company's needs. And so I don't know, I think that was just a realization that I had as I was thinking through this podcast, and I think that's partly why I haven't done too much public speaking.
turns.zh: 不，这超棒。我希望对你听众有用。我会说过去几天，当我为这准备，我 honest 有点 anxious 关于我有没有足够深的独立框架需要想出？但就 authentic 对我这些公司的真实经验，我的很多所学是 off 其他试过类似事并成功或失败的人。而我觉得重要的是你有那 mental sponge。你能试一堆不同事、你能吸收它们然后立刻实践、discard 不 work 的、为你自己和公司需要演化它们。所以我不知道，我觉得那是我想过这播客时的 realization，而我觉得那部分 why 我没做太多公开演讲。

turns.speaker: Lenny
